Hands-on Exercise 2: Spatial Point Pattern Analysis

Overview

This page combines two Hands-on Exercise 2 topics:

  • First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
  • 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods

The two chapters use the same child care point data. Chapter 4 focuses on where the points are dense. Chapter 5 checks whether the points are spatially random or show interaction at different distances.

Note

The course examples use KML files. I use the downloaded GeoJSON files in this project. The important step is the same: both layers are transformed to EPSG:3414 before distance analysis.

Getting Started

Load Packages

library(sf)
library(terra)
library(spatstat)
library(tmap)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

set.seed(1234)
tmap_mode("plot")
tibble(
  package = c("sf", "terra", "spatstat", "tmap", "tidyverse"),
  version = c(
    as.character(packageVersion("sf")),
    as.character(packageVersion("terra")),
    as.character(packageVersion("spatstat")),
    as.character(packageVersion("tmap")),
    as.character(packageVersion("tidyverse"))
  )
) %>%
  kable()
package version
sf 1.1.0
terra 1.8.93
spatstat 3.6.2
tmap 4.2
tidyverse 2.0.0

These packages cover the full workflow. sf handles vector data, spatstat handles point pattern analysis, and tmap is used for map output.

Data Used

data_used <- tibble(
  data_type = c("Geospatial", "Geospatial"),
  file = c(
    "Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)",
    "Child Care Services"
  ),
  path = c(
    "data/geospatial/master_plan_2019_subzone_no_sea.geojson",
    "data/geospatial/childcare_services.geojson"
  ),
  source = c("data.gov.sg", "data.gov.sg")
)

kable(data_used)
data_type file path source
Geospatial Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) data/geospatial/master_plan_2019_subzone_no_sea.geojson data.gov.sg
Geospatial Child Care Services data/geospatial/childcare_services.geojson data.gov.sg

The boundary layer gives the study area. The child care layer gives the point events for the analysis.

Part 1: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis

First-order analysis is mainly about intensity. In simple terms, I am asking where child care services are more concentrated.

Import and Transform Geospatial Data

mpsz_sf <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/master_plan_2019_subzone_no_sea.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

childcare_sf <- st_read(
  "data/geospatial/childcare_services.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
layer_summary <- tibble(
  layer = c("mpsz_sf", "childcare_sf"),
  features = c(nrow(mpsz_sf), nrow(childcare_sf)),
  geometry_type = c(
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(mpsz_sf)), collapse = ", "),
    paste(unique(st_geometry_type(childcare_sf)), collapse = ", ")
  ),
  epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz_sf)$epsg, st_crs(childcare_sf)$epsg)
)

kable(layer_summary)
layer features geometry_type epsg
mpsz_sf 332 MULTIPOLYGON 3414
childcare_sf 1925 POINT 3414

EPSG:3414 uses metres. This matters because nearest neighbour distance and KDE bandwidth both depend on distance units.

Map the Child Care Services

tm_shape(mpsz_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey70", lwd = 0.3) +
  tm_shape(childcare_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.03, col = "#2b8cbe", alpha = 0.55) +
  tm_title("Child Care Services in Singapore")

The points are not evenly spread across the island. They are mostly in residential planning areas, which is expected for this type of facility.

Convert sf Data to ppp

coords <- st_coordinates(childcare_sf)

childcare_ppp <- ppp(
  x = coords[, "X"],
  y = coords[, "Y"],
  window = as.owin(st_bbox(mpsz_sf))
)

class(childcare_ppp)
[1] "ppp"

The course uses as.ppp(childcare_sf). In my current spatstat setup, I create the same ppp object explicitly from the point coordinates.

tibble(
  total_points = npoints(childcare_ppp),
  duplicated_xy = sum(duplicated(as.data.frame(coords))),
  window_type = childcare_ppp$window$type
) %>%
  kable()
total_points duplicated_xy window_type
1925 187 rectangle

Some centres share the same coordinate. This can happen when several services are in the same building.

Create the Singapore Study Window

mpsz_cl <- st_union(st_geometry(mpsz_sf))
sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)

class(sg_owin)
[1] "owin"
plot(sg_owin, main = "Singapore study window")

The owin object tells spatstat where the study area is. Without it, the point pattern would only know the rectangular bounding box.

Combine Points and Window

childcareSG_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[sg_owin])

childcareSG_ppp
Planar point pattern: 1925 points
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 56396.44] x [15748.72, 50256.33] units
window_summary <- tibble(
  points = npoints(childcareSG_ppp),
  window_type = Window(childcareSG_ppp)$type,
  window_area_sqkm = spatstat.geom::area.owin(Window(childcareSG_ppp)) / 1000000,
  average_intensity_per_sqkm = intensity(childcareSG_ppp) * 1000000
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

kable(window_summary)
points window_type window_area_sqkm average_intensity_per_sqkm
1925 polygonal 784.784 2.453

Now the point pattern is clipped to the Singapore boundary. This is the object used in the nearest neighbour and density analysis.

Clark-Evans Test

ce_global_z <- clarkevans.test(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "clustered"
)

ce_global_z

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.49444, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)

The Clark-Evans R value is below 1. This means the child care services are closer together than a random pattern.

ce_global_mc <- clarkevans.test(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "clustered",
  method = "MonteCarlo",
  nsim = 99
)

ce_global_mc

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 99 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.49444, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)

The Monte Carlo test gives the same broad conclusion. The observed pattern is more clustered than Complete Spatial Randomness.

Kernel Density Estimation

kde_SG_diggle <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

plot(kde_SG_diggle, main = "KDE of child care services, bw.diggle")

KDE turns point locations into a smooth surface. High values show places with stronger concentration of child care services.

bw <- bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)
bw
   sigma 
295.4419

The bandwidth controls how smooth the density surface is. A larger bandwidth makes a smoother map.

Rescale KDE Values

childcareSG_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(
  childcareSG_ppp,
  1000,
  "km"
)
kde_childcareSG_km <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.diggle,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "KDE after rescaling to kilometres")

Rescaling makes the distance unit easier to read. The pattern is the same, but the bandwidth is now expressed in kilometres.

Compare Bandwidth Methods

bw_scott <- bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp_km)

bandwidth_table <- tibble(
  method = c("bw.CvL", "bw.scott x", "bw.scott y", "bw.ppl", "bw.diggle"),
  sigma_km = c(
    as.numeric(bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
    as.numeric(bw_scott["sigma.x"]),
    as.numeric(bw_scott["sigma.y"]),
    as.numeric(bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
    as.numeric(bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km))
  )
) %>%
  mutate(sigma_km = round(sigma_km, 3))

kable(bandwidth_table)
method sigma_km
bw.CvL 4.543
bw.scott x 2.160
bw.scott y 1.396
bw.ppl 0.390
bw.diggle 0.295

Different methods choose different bandwidths. I keep bw.diggle for most maps because it gives a clear local pattern without being too rough.

kde_childcareSG_ppl <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = bw.ppl,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_km, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ppl, main = "bw.ppl")
par(old_par)

bw.ppl uses a larger bandwidth here, so the density surface is smoother. bw.diggle keeps more local detail.

Compare Kernel Methods

sigma_km <- as.numeric(bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km))

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
  main = "Gaussian"
)
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "epanechnikov"),
  main = "Epanechnikov"
)
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "quartic"),
  main = "Quartic"
)
plot(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sigma_km, edge = TRUE, kernel = "disc"),
  main = "Disc"
)
par(old_par)

Changing the kernel changes the surface shape slightly. The main hotspot pattern remains similar.

Fixed and Adaptive KDE

kde_childcareSG_fb <- density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  sigma = 0.6,
  edge = TRUE,
  kernel = "gaussian"
)

kde_childcareSG_ab <- adaptive.density(
  childcareSG_ppp_km,
  method = "kernel"
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG_fb, main = "Fixed bandwidth, 0.6 km")
plot(kde_childcareSG_ab, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")
par(old_par)

Fixed bandwidth uses one smoothing distance everywhere. Adaptive bandwidth changes the smoothing by local point density.

Cartographic KDE Map

kde_childcareSG_terra <- terra::rast(kde_SG_diggle)
crs(kde_childcareSG_terra) <- "EPSG:3414"

kde_childcareSG_terra
class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 128, 128, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 419.757, 269.5907  (x, y)
extent      : 2667.538, 56396.44, 15748.72, 50256.33  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414) 
source(s)   : memory
name        :         lyr.1 
min value   : -9.662620e-21 
max value   :  3.727443e-05 
unit        :          unit

I use the metre-based KDE here so the raster coordinates match EPSG:3414.

tm_shape(kde_childcareSG_terra) +
  tm_raster(
    col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "viridis"),
    col.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Density values",
      title.size = 0.7,
      text.size = 0.7,
      bg.color = "white",
      bg.alpha = 0.75,
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
      frame = TRUE
    )
  ) +
  tm_compass() +
  tm_layout(scale = 1.0)

This is a cleaner map output. It shows the KDE result as a raster surface instead of a basic R plot.

First-order Analysis by Planning Area

make_area_window <- function(planning_area) {
  mpsz_sf %>%
    filter(PLN_AREA_N == planning_area) %>%
    st_geometry() %>%
    st_union() %>%
    as.owin()
}

make_area_area <- function(planning_area) {
  mpsz_sf %>%
    filter(PLN_AREA_N == planning_area) %>%
    st_geometry() %>%
    st_union() %>%
    st_area() %>%
    as.numeric()
}

pg_owin <- make_area_window("PUNGGOL")
tm_owin <- make_area_window("TAMPINES")
ck_owin <- make_area_window("CHOA CHU KANG")
jw_owin <- make_area_window("JURONG WEST")

childcare_pg_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[pg_owin])
childcare_tm_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[tm_owin])
childcare_ck_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[ck_owin])
childcare_jw_ppp <- unmark(childcare_ppp[jw_owin])
planning_area_summary <- tibble(
  planning_area = c("Punggol", "Tampines", "Choa Chu Kang", "Jurong West"),
  childcare_points = c(
    npoints(childcare_pg_ppp),
    npoints(childcare_tm_ppp),
    npoints(childcare_ck_ppp),
    npoints(childcare_jw_ppp)
  ),
  area_sqkm = c(
    make_area_area("PUNGGOL"),
    make_area_area("TAMPINES"),
    make_area_area("CHOA CHU KANG"),
    make_area_area("JURONG WEST")
  ) / 1000000
) %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqkm = round(area_sqkm, 2),
    points_per_sqkm = round(childcare_points / area_sqkm, 2)
  )

kable(planning_area_summary)
planning_area childcare_points area_sqkm points_per_sqkm
Punggol 72 9.37 7.68
Tampines 117 20.80 5.62
Choa Chu Kang 74 6.12 12.09
Jurong West 110 14.68 7.49

These four planning areas have enough points for local comparison. The point count alone is not enough, so I also calculate points per square kilometre.

childcare_pg_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_tm_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_jw_ppp_km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_jw_ppp, 1000, "km")
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(childcare_pg_ppp_km, main = "Punggol")
plot(childcare_tm_ppp_km, main = "Tampines")
plot(childcare_ck_ppp_km, main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(childcare_jw_ppp_km, main = "Jurong West")
par(old_par)

This local view makes the point pattern easier to inspect. The whole-island view hides many small differences.

Clark-Evans Test by Planning Area

ce_ck <- clarkevans.test(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

ce_tm <- clarkevans.test(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  correction = "none",
  clipregion = NULL,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)

ce_ck

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcare_ck_ppp
R = 0.84097, p-value = 0.008866
alternative hypothesis: two-sided
ce_tm

    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcare_tm_ppp
R = 0.66817, p-value = 6.58e-12
alternative hypothesis: two-sided
area_ce_table <- tibble(
  planning_area = c("Choa Chu Kang", "Tampines"),
  R = c(unname(ce_ck$statistic), unname(ce_tm$statistic)),
  p_value = format.pval(
    c(ce_ck$p.value, ce_tm$p.value),
    digits = 3,
    eps = 0.001
  )
) %>%
  mutate(R = round(R, 3))

kable(area_ce_table)
planning_area R p_value
Choa Chu Kang 0.841 0.00887
Tampines 0.668 < 0.001

Both R values are below 1. This suggests clustering at the planning area level too.

KDE by Planning Area

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(
  density(childcare_pg_ppp_km, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
  main = "Punggol"
)
plot(
  density(childcare_tm_ppp_km, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
  main = "Tampines"
)
plot(
  density(childcare_ck_ppp_km, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
  main = "Choa Chu Kang"
)
plot(
  density(childcare_jw_ppp_km, sigma = bw.diggle, edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"),
  main = "Jurong West"
)
par(old_par)

The KDE maps show local high-density areas. This is more useful than only saying whether the whole pattern is clustered.

Part 2: Second-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis

Second-order analysis looks at distance relationships between points. Here I use Choa Chu Kang and Tampines because they have enough child care points and the course also uses them.

Note

The course uses 999 simulations for some CSR tests. I use simulation_n <- 99 so the page can render faster. The code structure is the same, and a larger number can be used for a final statistical run.

simulation_n <- 99
gf_rmax <- 500
kl_rmax <- 1000

G-function

The G-function looks at nearest neighbour distance from each observed point. If the observed curve rises faster than the CSR curve, nearby points are common.

G_CK <- Gest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "border", rmax = gf_rmax)
G_tm <- Gest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "best", rmax = gf_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(G_CK, xlim = c(0, gf_rmax), main = "G-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(G_tm, xlim = c(0, gf_rmax), main = "G-function: Tampines")
par(old_par)

The two plots show how quickly each child care centre finds another nearby centre.

G_CK_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Gest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

G_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Gest,
  correction = "all",
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(G_CK_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(G_tm_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Tampines")
par(old_par)

The envelope is the random benchmark. When the observed line moves outside the envelope, the pattern is not behaving like CSR at that distance.

F-function

The F-function uses random empty locations and measures the distance to the nearest child care point. It helps describe empty space.

F_CK <- Fest(childcare_ck_ppp, rmax = gf_rmax)
F_tm <- Fest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "best", rmax = gf_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(F_CK, main = "F-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(F_tm, main = "F-function: Tampines")
par(old_par)

If the F curve rises quickly, most places are close to a child care service. This is about coverage from the empty-space side.

F_CK_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Fest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

F_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Fest,
  correction = "all",
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rmax = gf_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(F_CK_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(F_tm_csr, main = "CSR envelope: Tampines")
par(old_par)

This adds a random reference to the empty-space analysis. It is useful because a visual curve alone can be hard to judge.

K-function

The K-function counts neighbours within increasing distance bands. It is useful for checking clustering across many distances.

K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)
K_tm <- Kest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "K-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(K_tm, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "K-function: Tampines")
par(old_par)

The transformed plot makes it easier to compare the observed pattern with the CSR reference line.

K_ck_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Kest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

K_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Kest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(K_ck_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "K CSR: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(K_tm_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "K CSR: Tampines")
par(old_par)

For K-function envelopes, a line above the random envelope suggests clustering at that distance range.

L-function

The L-function is a transformed version of K. It is often easier to read because CSR is shown around zero after subtracting distance.

L_ck <- Lest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)
L_tm <- Lest(childcare_tm_ppp, correction = "Ripley", rmax = kl_rmax)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(L_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "L-function: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(L_tm, . - r ~ r, ylab = "L(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)", main = "L-function: Tampines")
par(old_par)

L-function is easier to explain visually. Values above zero usually indicate clustering.

L_ck_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_ck_ppp,
  Lest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

L_tm_csr <- envelope(
  childcare_tm_ppp,
  Lest,
  nsim = simulation_n,
  rank = 1,
  global = TRUE,
  rmax = kl_rmax,
  verbose = FALSE
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(L_ck_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "L CSR: Choa Chu Kang")
plot(L_tm_csr, . - theo ~ r, main = "L CSR: Tampines")
par(old_par)

The CSR envelopes help confirm that the pattern is not only a visual impression. The services show clustering at short distances, especially in denser residential parts.

Final Reflection

This hands-on exercise shows two ways to study point patterns. First-order methods show where the intensity is high. Second-order methods check how points relate to other points across distance. For child care services, clustering is expected because centres follow housing estates and population demand. The main limitation is that CSR is a simple benchmark, so the result should be read as an exploratory test rather than a full explanation of why centres are located there.
